note: Plain language definitions of the zoning districts that appear in application briefs.

R1.d: The lowest density residential district. Single family detached houses on large lots.

R2.d: Single family detached houses, smaller lots than R1.

R3.d: Low density. Single and two family houses, detached, semi detached or attached depending on the suffix.

R4.d: Low density. Single and two family houses, and small apartment houses in some subdistricts.

R5.d: Low to moderate density. Small apartment houses and attached houses.

R6.d: Moderate density. Apartment buildings are permitted. Common across brownstone Brooklyn.

R7.d: Medium density apartment buildings, taller than R6.

R8.d: High density apartment buildings, substantially more than R7.

R10.d: The highest density residential district. Tall apartment towers.

R11.d: High density, created for specific large scale sites.

R12.d: The densest residential district, used in a small number of places.

C1.d: A local retail overlay mapped on top of a residential district. Corner shops and services, usually capped at 10,000 square feet per establishment.

C2.d: A local service overlay on a residential district. Slightly broader than C1, still local in scale.

C3.d: Waterfront recreation. Boating and beach related uses. Very little retail.

C4.d: Regional shopping outside the central business districts. Department stores, theatres, larger retail.

C5.d: A central business district serving the whole region. Offices and high end retail. Housing permitted.

C6.d: A central business district allowing a wide range of commercial uses, offices and housing at high density.

C7.d: Large open amusement parks. No housing.

C8.d: Heavy service and automotive. Repair shops, warehouses, car washes. No housing.

M1.d: Light manufacturing with the strictest performance standards for noise, odour, vibration and emissions. Often a buffer between heavier industry and residential areas.

M2.d: Medium manufacturing. Looser performance standards than M1.

M3.d: Heavy manufacturing, for uses with the greatest nuisance potential. Usually on the waterfront.

suffix.A: Contextual. Height, setback and street wall are tightly controlled so new buildings match the existing streetscape.
suffix.B: Contextual and lower scale than the A version of the same district.
suffix.X: Contextual, allowing greater height in exchange for a narrower tower above the base.
suffix.H: A special variant used in a limited area.

MX.d: Written as two codes with a slash, such as M1-2A/R7A. Both sets of rules apply on the same lots, so residential and light industrial uses are permitted together. This is the mechanism that lets a manufacturing area take housing without giving up its industrial designation. The MX number identifies which paired district it is in the Zoning Resolution.

MIH.d: Where mapped, a share of new housing must be permanently affordable at set income bands. It is mapped through a zoning text amendment to Appendix F, which is why rezoning applications almost always carry one alongside the map change.

numbers: In residential and commercial districts the number is density: a higher number means more can be built. In manufacturing districts the number is how heavy the permitted industry is, so M3 allows heavier uses than M1, and it says nothing about how much can be built.
